evidence.claim: From Tioga Pass, the highway drops more than three thousand feet
evidence.quote: losing more than 3,000 ft (910 m) by the time the road reaches U.S. Route 395.

evidence.claim: The Lee Vining Canyon drive descends the Sierra Nevada’s steep eastern side, losing more than 3,000 feet in approximately 12 miles.
evidence.quote: East of Tioga Pass, the highway begins a dramatic descent through Lee Vining Canyon, dropping more than 3,000 feet (910 m) over approximately 12 miles (19 km) as it descends the steep eastern escarpment of the Sierra Nevada.

evidence.claim: It begins at Tioga Pass, 9,945 feet above sea level, and reaches US 395 at Lee Vining beside Mono Lake.
evidence.quote: Tioga Pass, at 9,945 feet (3,031 m)

evidence.claim: It begins at Tioga Pass, 9,945 feet above sea level, and reaches US 395 at Lee Vining beside Mono Lake.
evidence.quote: The canyon road ends at the community of Lee Vining, on the southwestern shore of Mono Lake, where SR 120 meets US 395.

evidence.claim: This section of Route 120 is the Lee Vining Canyon Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway administered by Inyo National Forest.
evidence.quote: This segment through Lee Vining Canyon is designated as the Lee Vining Canyon Scenic Byway, a National Forest Scenic Byway administered by the Inyo National Forest.

evidence.claim: The western approach to the pass is gradual; east of the summit, the road drops sharply toward the basin.
evidence.quote: This pass, like many other passes in the Sierra Nevada, has a gradual approach from the west and drops off to the east dramatically

evidence.claim: The wider Tioga Road crossing began in 1883 as a road to silver mines east of the pass and later became a private toll road.
evidence.quote: The Tioga Road was built in 1883 as a mining road to reach the Sheepherder and Tioga silver mines east of Tioga Pass. It became a private toll road

evidence.claim: In 1915, Stephen Mather bought the road with his own money and donations from the Sierra Club and Modesto Chamber of Commerce, enabling public access through Yosemite’s high country.
evidence.quote: In 1915, Stephen Mather, who would become the first director of the National Park Service, purchased the road for $15,000 using his own funds and donations from the Sierra Club and the Modesto Chamber of Commerce, enabling public access through the park's high country.

evidence.claim: On the eastern approach, builders working along Lee Vining Canyon’s sheer walls in the 1930s faced the crossing’s most difficult construction.
evidence.quote: Due to the ruggedness of the area, the construction of the road along the sheer canyon walls during the 1930s was the most difficult part of the trans-Sierra crossing.

evidence.claim: From the pass’s stone entrance buildings, follow Route 120 toward Tioga Lake, a glacial lake beside the highway.
evidence.quote: Both are rustic stone structures with peeled log roof structures

evidence.claim: From the pass’s stone entrance buildings, follow Route 120 toward Tioga Lake, a glacial lake beside the highway.
evidence.quote: Tioga Lake is a small glacial lake in the Inyo National Forest of Mono County, California, about two miles (3 km) north of the Tioga Pass entrance to Yosemite National Park. The lake bed is alongside State Route 120

evidence.claim: Farther down, Lee Vining Creek drops from Ellery Lake into the canyon and continues toward Mono Lake.
evidence.quote: It flows southeast to Ellery Lake, a natural lake enlarged by a dam, where it turns east and drops over Ellery Lake Falls into the deep Lee Vining Canyon. From there, it flows eastwards out of the mountains past the small town of Lee Vining. The creek terminates at a small sandy delta on the western shore of Mono Lake.

evidence.claim: The road finishes at Lee Vining, at the eastern base of the Sierra.
evidence.quote: Lee Vining is in western Mono County along U.S. Route 395, at the eastern base of the Sierra Nevada.

evidence.claim: Tioga Pass’s entrance buildings use heavy stone and logs at Yosemite’s eastern gateway.
evidence.quote: The Tioga Pass Entrance Station is the primary entrance for travelers entering Yosemite National Park from the east on the Tioga Pass Road.

evidence.claim: Tioga Pass’s entrance buildings use heavy stone and logs at Yosemite’s eastern gateway.
evidence.quote: Both are rustic stone structures with peeled log roof structures

evidence.claim: The ranger station dates to 1931 and the comfort station to 1934; Civilian Conservation Corps workers assisted with construction.
evidence.quote: a ranger station and a comfort station, built in 1931 and 1934 respectively.

evidence.claim: The ranger station dates to 1931 and the comfort station to 1934; Civilian Conservation Corps workers assisted with construction.
evidence.quote: Civilian Conservation Corps workers assisted in the entrance station's construction.

evidence.claim: Stone construction here set a precedent for other buildings in Yosemite’s high country.
evidence.quote: The use of stone at Tioga Pass set a precedent for the extensive employment of stone construction in other park buildings in the Yosemite high country.

evidence.claim: The ranger station sits into the hillside, with a porch across most of its front and massive timber window lintels.
evidence.quote: set into the slope of the hillside with a porch extending across most of the front.

evidence.claim: The ranger station sits into the hillside, with a porch across most of its front and massive timber window lintels.
evidence.quote: Window lintels are single massive shaped timbers.

evidence.claim: The log gates are replacements: after the original structures were removed, they were rebuilt in 1999 on surviving stone piers.
evidence.quote: Two log gate structures that had been removed since the site's original construction were rebuilt in 1999; the stone piers that supported them remain.

evidence.claim: The comfort station repeats the stone-and-log design, with sloping walls and a steeper roof.
evidence.quote: The comfort station is of similar design, with battered (sloping) stone walls, measuring about 11 feet (3.4 m) by 26 feet (7.9 m), with a steeper roof pitch

evidence.claim: Look for oversized stonework and heavy log framing at the ranger station’s porch.
evidence.quote: The masonry is oversized, with similarly heavy log porch and roof framing.

evidence.claim: Tioga Pass closes for winter snow. Opening and closing dates vary considerably from year to year.
evidence.quote: The pass is subject to winter closure due to high snowfall, normally from around the end of October until the end of May the following year, though these dates are subject to considerable variation.

evidence.claim: Tioga Lake lies beside Route 120 just north of Yosemite’s Tioga Pass entrance, a small glacial lake within Inyo National Forest.
evidence.quote: Tioga Lake is a small glacial lake in the Inyo National Forest of Mono County, California, about two miles (3 km) north of the Tioga Pass entrance to Yosemite National Park. The lake bed is alongside State Route 120

evidence.claim: Gaylor Peak rises above both the lake and the pass.
evidence.quote: The peak rises prominently above Tioga Pass and Tioga Lake

evidence.claim: Gaylor Peak’s summit consists of metamorphic rock, and the mountain is a fault block.
evidence.quote: The peak's geological composition consists of metamorphic rock, and it is classified as a fault block mountain.

evidence.claim: Runoff from its eastern side drains into Tioga Lake, then feeds Lee Vining Creek and ultimately Mono Lake.
evidence.quote: To the east, runoff drains into Tioga Lake, eventually feeding into Lee Vining Creek and ultimately reaching Mono Lake.

evidence.claim: The western drainage takes a different course, reaching Gaylor Lakes and the Dana Fork of the Tuolumne River.
evidence.quote: Precipitation runoff from Gaylor Peak flows westward into Gaylor Lakes and then into the Dana Fork of the Tuolumne River.

evidence.claim: The lake’s high elevation and position near the pass make its weather unpredictable; frost is possible even in July.
evidence.quote: Because of the altitude and its location at the crest of a major pass, the weather is extremely unpredictable. Frost is even possible in July.

evidence.claim: At the foot of the canyon, Lee Vining has carried several names.
evidence.quote: Lee Vining (formerly Leevining, Poverty Flat, and Lakeview)

evidence.claim: At the foot of the canyon, Lee Vining has carried several names.
evidence.quote: Lee Vining is situated near the foot of Lee Vining Canyon.

evidence.claim: Chris Mattly laid out the town as Lakeview in 1926, but a post-office application revealed that another California town already used the name.
evidence.quote: In 1926, the town was laid out by Chris Mattly and named "Lakeview", but when a post office was sought in 1928, it was learned that another town, Lakeview, California, already had the name.

evidence.claim: Lee Vining was chosen in 1953, honoring Leroy Vining, who established a mining camp here in 1852.
evidence.quote: The town was named after Leroy Vining, who founded the town in 1852 as a mining camp.

evidence.claim: Lee Vining was chosen in 1953, honoring Leroy Vining, who established a mining camp here in 1852.
evidence.quote: The name of Lee Vining was chosen in 1953.

evidence.claim: An earlier nickname, Poverty Flat, reflected the place’s unfavorable conditions for agriculture.
evidence.quote: The place was also called "Poverty Flat" for its unfavorable conditions for agriculture.

evidence.claim: The town stands on Mono Lake’s southwest shore, where tourism now supplies much of its economy.
evidence.quote: Lee Vining is located on the southwest shore of Mono Lake.

evidence.claim: The town stands on Mono Lake’s southwest shore, where tourism now supplies much of its economy.
evidence.quote: The economy of Lee Vining relies largely on tourism

evidence.claim: One local landmark is the Upside-Down House, built by silent-film actress Nellie Bly O’Bryan.
evidence.quote: The town is the site of the Upside-Down House, a distinctive local landmark built by silent film actress Nellie Bly O'Bryan.
